sentences.text: Unlike most other members of its group, this dinosaur had a U-shaped snout.
It was a substantial sauropod that grew to be 17 meters long, 4.5 meters high, and weighed 15 tonnes.
Distinctive features include decorative markings along the eye socket rim, a broad joint at the back of the skull, and twisted structures on the upper back bones.
This animal holds the title of the oldest known neosauropod and is the sole confirmed diplodocoid discovered in East Asia.
Its specific name translates to 'amazing' in Mandarin because finding a relative of the Dicraeosauridae family in this region was completely unexpected.
A local sheep herder named Ma Yun found the bones in 2004.
After the find, Ma Yun informed local officials Yang Huozhu and Liu Hongan about the discovery.
Digging began at a site called Ciyaopu near Lingwu, uncovering parts of seven to ten sauropod skeletons.
The species was officially named Lingwulong shenqi in 2018 by a large team led by Xu Xing.
The genus name honors the place of Lingwu, while the species name means 'dragon' in Chinese.
Lingwulong represents one of the earliest examples of neosauropods and is the only definitive diplodocoid known from East Asia.
This creature belongs to the Saurischia class.
Its immediate ancestral group is Flagellicaudata.
Xu and colleagues included it in their 2018 family tree of Flagellicaudata.
Studies from 2025 suggest it is closely related to Cetiosauriscus and may sit outside the Flagellicaudata clade or within Diplodocidae.
It lived in Asia during the early to middle Jurassic, roughly between 178 and 168 million years ago.
Fossils were found in China within the Yanan Formation.
While the exact age is uncertain, it likely lived between the late Toarcian and Bajocian stages, with a midpoint around 174 million years ago.
The time range for this species spans from the Aalenian to the Callovian, covering 174.7 to 161.5 million years ago.
Dating of the Yanan Formation indicates a specific window between 174.0 and 171.7 million years ago.
However, some scientists believe the remains come from the Zhiluo Formation, which would make the animal younger, dating to the Bathonian or early Oxfordian.
There is an ongoing discussion about whether diplodocoids were missing from East Asia because the Turgai Sea blocked their path, a view supported by the East Asia Isolation Hypothesis.
The existence of Lingwulong questions this isolation theory by proving diplodocoids were present in East Asia during the Jurassic.
This discovery undermines previous assumptions about paleobiogeography by showing these dinosaurs inhabited East Asia in the Early Jurassic.
